extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in religious criticism and historical authenticity (readers of Paine's Age of Reason)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative criteria and standards used to judge the historical authenticity, authorship, and credibility of the New Testament narratives and epistles, as argued in a skeptical/polemic essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement among eyewitnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: If multiple persons are true eye- and ear-witnesses to the same scene, their independent accounts will agree as to time and place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "If four men are eye-witnesses and ear-witnesses to a scene, they will without any concert between them, agree as to time and place, when and where that scene happened." Use concordant details of time/place across accounts as a sign of genuine eyewitness testimony; glaring disagreement undermines eyewitness claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradictions disprove apostolic authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Contradictory accounts within the Gospels demonstrate that their writers could not have been the apostles they are ascribed to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Matthew places a meeting in Galilee while Luke/John place it in Jerusalem; such fundamental contradictions indicate the writers were not the purported eyewitness apostles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradictions disprove a concerted forgery
rubrics_metrics.description: If the books were a coordinated imposture, their separate relations would corroborate; widespread contradictions therefore show they were not produced in concerted deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The same contradictions that prove there has been no concert, prove also that the reporters had no knowledge of the fact..." Lack of mutual corroboration implies neither joint fabrication nor genuine eyewitnesshood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private appearances cannot serve as public evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Events claimed to prove a doctrine (e.g., resurrection or ascension) needed to be public and visible to preclude denial; private, secretive appearances are inadequate as evidentiary basis for public claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Words, whether declarations or promises, that passed in private... could not be evidence in public; it was therefore necessary that this last scene should preclude the possibility of denial and dispute... as public and as visible as the sun at noon-day." Use expectation of publicity for foundational miracles as a test of plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-person testimony is weak when unsupported
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reported by only one individual (even a claim about many witnesses) is weak evidence, especially if that individual previously disbelieved the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paul's statement about more than five hundred seeing Christ is treated as the testimony of one man, not five hundred; the essay notes this undermines the claim's credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspiration incompatible with contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Books claimed to be divinely inspired should not contain clear contradictions; presence of contradictions argues against inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "As to inspiration, it is altogether out of the question; we may as well attempt to unite truth and falsehood, as inspiration and contradiction." Use internal logical coherence as necessary for claims of divine inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Late compilation reduces authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Long lapse between events and the time writings were collected into a canon (300+ years) introduces extreme uncertainty about authorship and authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "There was no such book as the New Testament till more than three hundred years after the time that Christ is said to have lived." Greater temporal distance allows copying, alteration, and forgery; earlier, contiguous documentation is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunities and incentives for forgery increase likelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: When textual transmission is by hand and institutional incentives favor miraculous narratives, the probability of forgery or alteration is high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No printing meant copies could be altered at pleasure; the church's interest in power and revenue made miraculous and wonderful writings more likely to be preserved and voted into the canon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public vote does not establish authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions by councils or votes to include books in a canon do not substitute for independent proof of authentic authorship or truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "It was upon the vote of such as Athanasius that the Testament was decreed to be the word of God; and nothing can present to us a more strange idea than that of decreeing the word of God by vote." Use documentary provenance, not ecclesiastical decree, as primary evidence of authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary quality and required skill as evidence of authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Works requiring exceptional literary or technical skill (e.g., Homer, Euclid) are less likely to be successful forgeries under another's name; the comparatively poor quality of the Gospels suggests authorship could be by many, not the few canonical names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons: "The authenticity of Homer... is much better established than that of the New Testament..." If many ordinary writers could produce the text, authorship attribution is more doubtful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patterns of credulity and legend formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports of apparitions and post-mortem visions commonly arise after violent or extraordinary deaths through credulity and compounding retellings; such social-psychological processes can explain the origin of resurrection stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues apparition stories (e.g., of Julius Caesar) and the tendency of compassion/credulity to 'stretch' narratives explain the genesis of the resurrection tales; consider sociocultural mechanisms for legend formation when assessing miraculous claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal narrative impossibilities and absurdities weaken credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixtures of incompatible features in reported events (e.g., vanishing and physical eating; grave-clothes left behind but no clothing accounted for at ascension) indicate legendary or invented storytelling rather than factual reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: Christ "vanishing out of sight" yet later "hungry, sits down to meat, and eats his supper"; failure to account for grave-clothes after resurrection. Use such narrative incoherencies to question literal historicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse of prophecy and typology undermines claim of fulfillment
rubrics_metrics.description: Retroactive application or twisting of earlier texts (types/prophecies) to fit later events is suspect; prophetic citations must be contextually appropriate to be reliable evidence of predictive fulfillment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Isaiah's sign to Ahaz misapplied as a messianic prophecy; Jonah treated as a type of Christ despite timing and factual mismatches (e.g., three days vs ~36 hours). Check original contexts and plausibility of typological links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity or uncertain authorship reduces credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When original manuscripts are not extant and authorship cannot be established, strong doubt should attach to claims of authoritative provenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The originals are not in the possession of any Christian Church existing... there is no possibility of proving the hand-writing..." Lack of authentic originals and later attributions should be treated as substantial negative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral character of proclaimers affects evidentiary weight
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral or psychological profile of principal advocates (e.g., fanaticism, prior persecution) influences the reliability of their testimony for religious claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of Paul: his zeal and prior persecution of Christians make him a poor moral evidence for the doctrines he later preaches; consider character and motivations of witnesses when weighing testimony.
